facts_from_discussion: Petitioner has neither argued that section 7491(a) applies nor established that its requirements have been met.

Surplus & Adventure: the court found that petitioner's testimony and documentary evidence substantiate the advertising/marketing expenses of $1,092.37, PayPal fees of $1,077.77, Penske truck rental of $80.19, and FedEx/USPS shipping fees of $229.94.

Surplus & Adventure car and truck expenses: petitioner provided noncontemporaneous records and credible testimony, but kept no contemporaneous records of the amount of each separate expense, only noncontemporaneous estimates of business mileage, and the records did not include the date or business purpose of the miles driven.

Surplus & Adventure depreciation: petitioner testified he was eligible to claim depreciation on unidentified assets but did not prove the assets' depreciable bases, useful lives, or previously allowable depreciation.
Fibre Arts: the court found that petitioner's testimony and documentary evidence substantiate Etsy selling fees of $202.90 and Ohio business filing fees of $145.15.
Fibre Arts car and truck expenses: petitioner kept only a noncontemporaneous summary log of estimated miles driven, without the dates and business purposes of the trips.

Fibre Arts depreciation: petitioner testified he was eligible to depreciate two embroidery machines, a generator, and a trailer used for Fibre Arts, but did not prove their depreciable bases, useful lives, or previously allowable depreciation.

STEAM Works: considering all the facts and circumstances, the court found that petitioner did not conduct STEAM Works in a businesslike manner and did not engage in it with an actual and honest profit objective during 2017; STEAM Works had no gross income in 2017.

Beavercreek property: respondent conceded that petitioner rented out the Beavercreek property as a business for five months of 2017; for the other seven months petitioner either did not rent it out or lived in it as his personal residence. Neither party asserted that section 280A applies to the Beavercreek property. Petitioner and his wife each paid half of its real estate taxes and mortgage interest; petitioner received the rental income and paid the expenses in the owner activity statement.

Beavercreek car and truck expenses: petitioner provided a summary "Auto & Travel Log" with estimated cost and miles for his various rental properties and repair receipts for two vehicles; the mileage evidence is a combined summary for his businesses and rental properties without dates or business purposes.

Beavercreek meals expenses: petitioner's evidence was a spreadsheet headed "Groceries" and "Restaurants" listing dates, property location, and "lunch" or a store/restaurant name, plus bank and credit card records; none of the records stated a business purpose.

Beavercreek depreciation: petitioner testified to a depreciation deduction "[i]n the range of $3,000" but did not provide the property's depreciable basis, useful life, or previously allowable depreciation.

Maryland property: the property was rented during all of 2017 and was jointly owned by petitioner and his wife, who each paid half of its real estate taxes and mortgage interest. Petitioner received the rental income and paid the expenses in the yearend statement, and paid hazard insurance of $845.48.

Maryland car and truck expenses: petitioner testified he drove one vehicle for several businesses and the Maryland property and submitted vehicle repair receipts and an estimated-mileage spreadsheet; he kept no contemporaneous records of each expense, and the records lacked dates and business purposes.
Maryland meals expenses: the same kind of "Groceries"/"Restaurants" spreadsheet plus bank and credit card statements, with no business purpose recorded.

Maryland depreciation: petitioner testified he should be entitled to depreciation on the house and on a fence but did not provide the property's depreciable basis, useful life, or previously allowable depreciation.

Late filing: petitioner's 2017 return, after the extension, was due October 15, 2018, and he did not file by that date; the IRS prepared the 2017 return under section 6020(b). Petitioner does not claim he filed timely; he argues only that he owes no deficiency for 2017. The court found petitioner has not shown reasonable cause for failing to timely file his 2017 return.
